message.reasoning:
We need to evaluate student submission against rubric criteria C1-C4 and requirements R1-R11.

Let's parse the document.

Executive summary: describes mission: Earth observation satellite for coral reef and ocean monitoring, fluid lensing tool, retrograde sun-synchronous polar orbit, low altitude, constant sun angle, operated from Australia, designed for Great Barrier Reef. Mentions STK simulations etc.

Introduction: mission concept/rationale. Coral reefs importance, GBR, bleaching. Need for dedicated satellite monitoring. Fluid lensing. Then "Other Earth observation satellites use networks or constellations... The ZYZZsat however, does not require such constant coverage... Thus, only one satellite is required." Users: "would likely be used by governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM) for research and/or education. Funding ... Australian University or Australian Government." So addresses primary mission, why needed, number (one) and why, users (operator/customers somewhat vague).

Mission design: Launch. Discusses piggybacking, factors, compares Vega VV18 and Falcon 9. Selects Vega E from Guiana Space Centre (Kourou, 5.05N). Justifies.

Orbit: SSO, low Earth, altitude 600 km, inclination 97.79°, COE table: a=6971 km, e=0, i=97.79°, RAAN 27.33°, argument of latitude 0°. Mentions J2 perturbation, sun-synchronous. Plots inclination vs altitude. Screenshots STK 3D view.

Ground control: Mount Pleasant Radio Observatory (Tasmania), owned by University of Tasmania. Access summary table from STK with durations, mean 580.786 sec (~9.7 min), frequent passes. Ground tracks images. States communication frequency? Table shows 15 accesses over ~3 days (Feb 3-5), ~6 per day? Actually 6 passes per day roughly. Average contact ~10 min. So communication frequency addressed.

Mission duration & EOL: 5 years, 2025-2030. EOL: uncontrolled deorbit, drag sail passive strategy. Mentions graveyard orbit alternative.

Conclusion: summary.

Bibliography: 10 references, some URLs, Wikipedia not acceptable? Reference [6] is Wikipedia "2021 in spaceflight". The task says Wikipedia is not an acceptable source. They use it for launch comparison. So referencing issue. Also references not formatted properly (just URLs, no titles/dates). Some reference numbers seem odd: "[10 d. ]" etc. But conversion artefacts maybe.

Requirements:
R1: propose simple mission benefits Australia, explain primary mission, overview, rationale. Yes, introduction.
R2: one or multiple spacecraft. Yes, one satellite and why.
R3: users, operator and customers. Partially: says likely used by governmental and science agencies (CSIRO, BOM), funding by university/government. Operator not explicitly stated? "operated and accessed from Australia ground facilities" executive summary. But not clear who operates. Maybe adequate partial.
R4: launch site and vehicle. Yes, Vega E from Guiana Space Centre.
R5: orbit type, characteristics, orbital elements. Yes, SSO, altitude, inclination, COE table. Good.
R6: orbital manoeuvres required? Says only orbital manoeuvre occurs at EOL, explained in EOL. EOL is deorbit via drag sail (no thrusters). So no manoeuvres during mission except EOL passive. Describes. Meets.
R7: ground-control facilities and communication frequency. Yes, Mt Pleasant, access summary with frequency/duration. Meets.
R8: mission duration and EOL. Yes, 5 years, EOL plan drag sail. Meets.
R9: use mission-design software. Uses STK 11, screenshots. Yes.
R10: screenshots and provide STK files. Screenshots included (images 1-5). STK files? Not included in submission text; requirement says provide all relevant STK files. The submission only has report text and images, no files. So partial? The PDF may have appendix? Not shown. Since only text given, we can't assume files. The requirement says "provide all relevant STK or PIGI files." In the document, no mention of attached files. So likely not met fully. But they have screenshots. We'll mark partial (screenshots yes, files not evident).
R11: clear logical structure, concise, cite borrowed material. Structure has headings, but length? References poor, Wikipedia used, not properly formatted. So partial.

Technical correctness:
- Launch: Vega E not built yet, first launch 2024; they acknowledge. But Vega E from Kourou; Vega E likely can launch to SSO. But they chose 2025. Fine.
- Orbit: 600 km, inclination 97.79°. For SSO at 600 km, typical inclination ~97.8°, yes. But they say "altitude of 600km requires mean inclination of 97.7924°" from plot. That's plausible. Semi-major axis 6971 km (6371+600=6971) correct. RAAN 27.33° "initial value indicates location of launch facility" - is that correct? RAAN is not directly launch site latitude; it's the longitude of ascending node in inertial space. It doesn't indicate launch facility location. That's technically incorrect. They say "The initial value indicates the location of the launch facility." This is wrong. Could be a significant error. Also RAAN will shift 360°/year; sun-synchronous. But initial RAAN chosen arbitrary. They don't justify 27.33°.
- They claim "sun-synchronous orbit inherently experiences significant J2 perturbations ... For orbit to be truly sun-synchronous, RAAN must change at rate 360° per year; ascending node experiencing 1° east-ward precession every day." That's correct.
- Orbit elements: argument of latitude 0° at epoch. But they don't specify true anomaly; they use argument of latitude. For circular orbit, that's fine. But they don't give epoch time. They have images dated 3 Feb 2025. Fine.
- Ground station: Mount Pleasant Radio Observatory in Tasmania. Is it suitable? It's a radio telescope, not a dedicated TT&C station. Could be used, but not typical for satellite communications. They claim large array of receivers. Possibly okay but not substantiated. They don't discuss link budget, data rate, frequencies. The task asks "how often will your spacecraft be able to communicate" - they give access times. But they don't discuss communication system (e.g., S-band/X-band) or data volume. But not explicitly required? The rubric includes "ground control facilities and how often communicate". They provide frequency and duration from STK. So okay.
- They say "average contact duration of almost ten minutes" from mean 580.786 sec = 9.68 min. Correct.
- They mention "The access periods define when satellite can communicate... actual image surveying ... will only occur in daytime... descending part of its orbit." For SSO with 600 km, descending node local time depends on RAAN. They don't specify local time of ascending node (LTAN). Sun-synchronous orbit has constant local time; to have daytime descending, need appropriate LTAN. They don't specify. But they imply descending is daytime. Could be okay if chosen. However, they don't give LTAN, which is important for SSO. Not in COE table. They just say "descending part where satellite is constantly in sunlight." For SSO at 600 km, orbital period ~96.7 min, eclipse fraction? At 600 km, typical eclipse ~35 min. Descending pass might be sunlit depending on LTAN. They haven't given LTAN. This is a gap.
- EOL: drag sail. For 600 km, drag sail can deorbit within 25 years? They don't quantify. But acceptable for preliminary.
- Mission duration 5 years; okay.

Figures:
Image 1 and 2: STK 3D view of orbit 12 hours apart. Good, shows orbit.
Image 3: Inclination vs altitude plot. Looks like generated. Good.
Image 4: DN ground track with ground station and satellite. Good.
Image 5: AN/DN ground track. Good.
Tables: Launch comparison tables from Wikipedia? They cite [6] Wikipedia timeline. The tables include references [49]-[74] which are Wikipedia's references, not theirs. They included table with footnote references but didn't cite properly. This is an issue: tables appear copied from Wikipedia without proper attribution? They cite [6] for the directory, but the table itself likely from Wikipedia. They have references in table but not in their bibliography. So potential plagiarism/citation issue. The rubric C4/R11 requires proper citation. They use Wikipedia, which is explicitly not acceptable. So that's a significant deficiency.

Now assess criteria:

C1 Introduction: mission concept and rationale. Includes primary mission, why needed, number of spacecraft and why, users. High standard? They give detailed descriptions, references [1]-[4]. Users somewhat vague. I'd say Accomplished but maybe lower end. Mark 7-8? It addresses all requirements. User identification: operator/customers somewhat implied but not explicit. Still, probably adequate to high. I'd give 7 or 8. Let's see: "The proposed satellite would likely be used by governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM) for research and/or education. Funding would likely be subsidised by either an Australian University or the Australian Government..." That's users (customers) but operator not clear. Executive summary says "operated and accessed from Australia ground facilities" but not who operates. Maybe partial. But overall C1 is good. I'd say 7 (Accomplished low) or 6 (Adequate high). Since it does address all, I'll give 7.

C2 Main body mission design: weight 60. Addresses launch, orbit, ground control, communications, duration/EOL. Uses STK screenshots and calculations. Technical errors: RAAN initial value wrong justification; no LTAN; missing link budget/data rate; launch vehicle not yet built; Wikipedia source for launch. But overall comprehensive. Evidence: screenshots, tables. I'd say Accomplished? The rubric says "Demonstrates high level understanding... Major requirements all addressed and well supported with quality evidence." The RAAN error is technical but perhaps minor. Lack of LTAN and communication details might reduce. But they did use software and show access. I'd rate Adequate to Accomplished. Since weight 60, need careful. I'd lean Adequate because of technical gaps: RAAN statement wrong, no explicit LTAN, no data rate/link budget, EOL drag sail not quantified, and reliance on Wikipedia for launch comparison. However, the design is fairly complete. The rubric's Adequate: "Design may be inconsistent with regards to purpose and clarity of thought or feature errors. Major requirements are addressed but may lack some detail or are not well supported with evidence." That fits. So C2 mark maybe 6 (Adequate top). Could be 7? But high level? I'd say 6. Let's see if any major requirement missing: R6 orbital manoeuvres: they say only EOL, but EOL is not a manoeuvre (passive drag). They don't mention any orbit insertion manoeuvre, assuming direct injection. That's plausible. R7 communication frequency: they give access data. Good. So all major requirements addressed. But quality evidence: STK screenshots yes, but no STK files; no hand calculations except inclination plot (software generated). Some evidence. I'd give 6.

C3 Conclusion: summarizes and reaches conclusions. It's brief but specific. Says launch may need adjustment, alternatives. Conclusions reached from evidence. I'd say Accomplished? It is detailed enough? It's a short paragraph but covers key points. Could be 7. Or Adequate 6. It lacks specific numbers but gives overall. I'll give 7.

C4 Report presentation: Structure clear with exec summary, intro, main body with subsections, conclusion, bibliography. Writing generally good but some informal/odd phrasing: "nicknamed ZYZZsat (Z-axis/Y-axis Zeroed Zoning Satellite)" maybe okay. "could be deemed a public service." Spelling/grammar okay. Figures labelled? They have captions under images: "STK 3D view of orbit: 12 hours apart", "DN path for orbits 1-15", etc. But images are not numbered in text? They are [Image 1] etc. from conversion, but original likely had figure numbers? The captions don't say "Figure 1". In the text they refer to "as seen below" etc. Tables have no table numbers or titles; they are just pasted tables. So formatting inconsistent. References: bibliography is a list of URLs, not properly formatted, no titles, authors, dates. Wikipedia used. In-text citations [1]-[10] but some references missing details. Reference [10] appears broken. Also they cite [6] for Wikipedia. So referencing poor. This fits Adequate or Deficient? The rubric: Accomplished requires references match, cited properly. Adequate: "References in text match reference list (and vice versa) and are mostly cited correctly." Deficient: "References are either not cited or cited inconsistently." Here they are cited but list is poor and Wikipedia not acceptable. I'd say Adequate at best. Mark 5 or 6. Presentation also lacks figure/table numbering and titles. So C4 = 5 or 6. I'll give 5 (Adequate mid) because of citation issues and formatting.

Requirements:
R1 yes.
R2 yes.
R3 partial (users identified but operator not explicit).
R4 yes.
R5 yes.
R6 yes (states no manoeuvres except EOL).
R7 yes.
R8 yes.
R9 yes (STK).
R10 partial (screenshots yes, STK files not evident).
R11 partial (structure good but referencing poor, Wikipedia, no file? Actually R11 about clear structure and citing borrowed material; they cite but poorly, Wikipedia unacceptable. So partial).

Technical issues:
- RAAN initial value incorrectly described as indicating launch facility location.
- No local time of ascending node (LTAN) specified for SSO, which determines lighting.
- No communication link budget or data rate analysis.
- Launch vehicle Vega E not yet operational; risk.
- Use of Wikipedia as source.
- Reference list incomplete/improper.
- Tables appear copied from Wikipedia without full attribution? Possibly.
- EOL drag sail not quantified (deorbit time).
- No STK files included (if not).

Overall: A solid preliminary design but with technical and referencing flaws.
